newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FEATURE - Tide of illegal immigration strains S.Africa.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Tide of illegal immigration strains S.Africa.

text.p: Herded by truncheon-wielding guards and barking dogs, young black men scurry in a line onto a train to sit with heads bowed as they wait for the start of the long trip back to Mozambique.
For another 500 illegal immigrants, a dream of a job and wealth in the new South Africa has ended at this dusty and dilapidated train station near Johannesburg.
Each week a train leaves Dyambu, a holding hostel at Krugersdorp, and heads for Mozambique's capital Maputo, loaded with illegal immigrants picked up by the South African police.
"They come here from all over the country, wherever the police pick them up," said Alan White, hostel manager at Dyambu.

For both immigrants and security guards the endless processing of documents and taking of finger prints has become a daily ritual. To relieve the tedium football matches are often arranged between the guards and those about to be shipped out.
A HUGE PROBLEM, BUT EXACT NUMBERS UNKNOWN
But though the problem is routine it poses a serious threat for South Africa's stuttering economy, just two and a half years after emerging from the darkness of the apartheid era.

The exact number of illegal immigrants in South Africa is unknown and estimates vary widely. A 1995 survey by the Human Sciences Research Council estimated their numbers at between 2.5 and 4.1 million.
Most come from neighbouring states like Mozambique and Zimbabwe, pushed out of their homes by poverty and pulled to the promised land of South Africa by the lure of industry and jobs.
South Africa, with its advanced infrastructure and large cities, is a powerful magnet for the poor of other African countries. But the burden of the massive illegal immigration is proving costly.
Most swarm into the teeming squatter camps surrounding all of South Africa's major cities and put a burden on the country's already stretched health, police and utility services.
"The economic concerns are rather severe in term of public services. We have to subsidise other countries' citizens," said David Galloway, group economist at Investec bank.
IMMIGRATION STRAINS ALREADY STUTTERING ECONOMY

South Africa is already staggering under an official unemployment rate of more than 30 percent. The flood of illegal immigrants has made the hunt for work -- even in the country's massive informal economy -- even harder.
"These people tend to take away work from locals and that is something South Africa cannot afford," Galloway said.
Social tension is rife as local South Africans accuse immigrants of taking their jobs, driving wages lower and becoming active in crime.
The flood of immigrants into the country contrasts sharply with the trickle of South Africans leaving it.

Those coming in are usually unskilled blacks looking to send money home, those leaving are mostly white professionals, quitting a country they see as having succumbed to violent crime or no longer offering them good career prospects.
"The labour coming in is unskilled. If it was highly skilled then we would probably turn a blind eye, but the only thing these immigrants are adding is a fiscal burden," Galloway said.
The Department of Home Affairs says the clandestine nature of the problem means it is impossible to say whether it is growing or not.

But democracy in South Africa, after decades of white minority rule, has made the country more attractive to migrant workers. At the same time job losses in the mining industry have meant once-legal overseas contract workers are now becoming illegal immigrants in order to get work.
GEOGRAPHICAL AND POLITICAL DIFFICULTIES

The nature of South Africa's long borders also makes holding the tide back difficult. South Africa touches Lesotho, Swaziland, Namibia, Botswana, Zimbabwe and Mozambique in a landscape characterised by mountain passes or trackless bush.
The South African Police Service, which has the tough job of patrolling the border, says the situation is not yet critical but that the frontier has to be tightened.
"The situation is of course under control, but there is always room for improvement," said police spokesman, Senior Superintendant Mohlabi Tlomatsana.
Talks are under way between the police, the armed forces and the Department of Home Affairs to work out a way in which the military can be brought in to help.
Aside from physical difficulties immigration is a political problem too.
Most of South Africa's neighbouring countries provided the African National Congress (ANC) with support during its long struggle against the former white regime.
Now the ANC is in power it is reluctant to forget its allies and start mass deportations of their citizens.
"These countries are happy to have these people coming here. There is a political debt and its payback time," Galloway said.
AMNESTY OFFERED BUT PROBLEM UNLIKELY TO DISAPPEAR

One way the ANC has sought to wriggle out of the problem is by offering an amnesty for those immigrants from the 12-nation Southern African Development Community who have lived in South Africa since 1991 and have jobs or South African partners.
Analysts say the amnesty, which has received 247,580 applications so far, may be a way of clearing the path for a future policy crackdown.
Whatever the future policy of the government, the problem will not go away by itself, as long as the huge disparity in wealth between South Africa and her neighbours remains.

As the train pulls out of Krugersdorp on its journey north another busload of immigrants is already arriving at the hostel. Some will almost certainly have been there before, but White says he sympathises with their plight.
"If you can't get enough money to feed your wife and family, you are going to try and do something about it," he said.
